items.stem: Which term matches this description: "DNA made by joining DNA from two different sources"?
items.answer: Recombinant DNA
items.markingKey: Recombinant DNA: DNA made by joining DNA from two different sources.

items.stem: Describe how a recombinant plasmid containing the human insulin gene is produced and inserted into bacteria.
items.answer: Obtain insulin mRNA from β cells, use reverse transcriptase to make cDNA, DNA polymerase for double strand; add promoter and sticky ends; cut plasmid with same restriction enzyme; mix, complementary sticky ends pair; DNA ligase seals; bacteria take up plasmids (heat shock with Ca²⁺ / electroporation); identify transformed bacteria with marker genes; culture in fermenters.
items.markingKey: cDNA via reverse transcriptase [1]; same restriction enzyme / sticky ends [1]; ligase [1]; transformation [1]; marker selection [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain why marker genes are needed in genetic engineering.
items.answer: Only a small proportion of cells take up the recombinant plasmid; markers (e.g. GFP or antibiotic resistance) allow those cells to be identified and selected.
items.markingKey: few cells transformed [1]; markers identify / select them [1] [2]

items.stem: A circular plasmid contains 2 recognition sites for HindIII. How many fragments are produced when it is cut completely?
items.markingKey: Circular: fragments = number of cuts = 2.

items.stem: EcoRI recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts it G^AATTC. The following single strand (5′→3′) of a linear double-stranded DNA molecule is to be cut: CCTTACCCTGTTTATGCGAATTCGAATGAATTCTGTTAGC. (a) Explain why the recognition site is described as palindromic. (b) Explain what is meant by sticky ends and why they are useful.
items.answer: (a) The sequence on one strand read 5′→3′ (GAATTC) is the same as the complementary strand read 5′→3′. (b) Staggered cuts leave short unpaired single-stranded overhangs; complementary overhangs from DNA cut with the same enzyme pair by hydrogen bonding, making joining easy.
items.markingKey: (a) The sequence on one strand read 5′→3′ (GAATTC) is the same as the complementary strand read 5′→3′ [1] (b) overhang / cut description [1]; complementary base pairing to join fragments [1] [2]

items.stem: SmaI recognises the sequence CCCGGG and cuts it CCC^GGG (blunt). The following single strand (5′→3′) of a linear double-stranded DNA molecule is to be cut: ATCGCTCCTCCCGGGGAGTGCCATTCCCGGGAAGCGTCGGGACTAGTCAA. (a) State how many SmaI sites are present and the lengths (in bases) of the fragments produced. (b) Explain why bacteria produce restriction enzymes.
items.answer: (a) 2 sites; fragments of 12, 16, 22 bases (b) To cut up the DNA of invading viruses (bacteriophages); their own DNA is protected by methylation.
items.markingKey: (a) sites located [1]; fragment lengths 12, 16, 22 [1] [2] (b) destroy viral DNA [1]; own DNA protected [1] [2]

items.stem: A company in Karachi produces erythropoietin for treating anaemia in kidney disease using genetically modified bacteria. (a) Describe how the cDNA is inserted into a plasmid. (b) Describe how bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid are identified.
items.answer: (a) Cut plasmid with a restriction enzyme; add matching sticky ends to cDNA (or cut with same enzyme); mix so sticky ends pair; DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds; promoter included. (b) The plasmid carries a marker gene such as GFP; colonies that fluoresce under UV light contain the plasmid; (or antibiotic resistance with replica plating).
items.markingKey: (a) same restriction enzyme [1]; complementary sticky ends [1]; ligase [1] [3] (b) marker gene [1]; detection method [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the principles of genetic engineering, using the production of human insulin by bacteria as an example.
items.answer: Obtain gene: mRNA from β cells → reverse transcriptase → cDNA → double-stranded; restriction enzymes cut plasmid, sticky ends; ligase; promoter; marker gene (GFP); transformation (Ca²⁺ heat shock); select transformed bacteria; culture in fermenter; extract and purify insulin; universal genetic code.
items.markingKey: obtaining gene [2]; vector and restriction enzymes [1]; ligase [1]; transformation [1]; markers [1]; production / code [1] [7]

items.stem: Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut both the plasmid and the gene to be inserted?
items.answer: To produce complementary sticky ends
items.markingKey: Same enzyme → same overhangs.

items.stem: A plasmid with one EcoRI site is cut with EcoRI. How many fragments are produced?
items.markingKey: A circular plasmid cut once gives one linear fragment.

items.stem: Explain why GFP is preferred to antibiotic resistance as a marker.
items.answer: GFP is detected simply by fluorescence without killing cells; avoids spreading antibiotic resistance genes to pathogenic bacteria.
items.markingKey: easy detection [1]; avoids spreading resistance [1] [2]

items.stem: A linear piece of DNA contains 2 recognition sites for HindIII. How many fragments are produced when it is cut completely?
items.markingKey: Linear: fragments = cuts + 1 = 3.

items.stem: A circular plasmid contains 4 recognition sites for SmaI. How many fragments are produced when it is cut completely?
items.markingKey: Circular: fragments = number of cuts = 4.

items.stem: A linear piece of DNA contains 4 recognition sites for BamHI. How many fragments are produced when it is cut completely?
items.markingKey: Linear: fragments = cuts + 1 = 5.

items.stem: BamHI recognises the sequence GGATCC and cuts it G^GATCC. The following single strand (5′→3′) of a linear double-stranded DNA molecule is to be cut: TGAAAAGGATCCTAGCGCTACCCGGATCCGGACTCCGTCA. (a) State how many BamHI sites are present and the lengths (in bases) of the fragments produced. (b) Explain why the recognition site is described as palindromic.
items.answer: (a) 2 sites; fragments of 7, 17, 16 bases (b) The sequence on one strand read 5′→3′ (GGATCC) is the same as the complementary strand read 5′→3′.
items.markingKey: (a) sites located [1]; fragment lengths 7, 17, 16 [1] [2] (b) The sequence on one strand read 5′→3′ (GGATCC) is the same as the complementary strand read 5′→3′ [1]

items.stem: A company in Kuala Lumpur produces human insulin for treating diabetes using genetically modified bacteria. (a) Describe how the cDNA is inserted into a plasmid. (b) Describe how bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid are identified.
items.answer: (a) Cut plasmid with a restriction enzyme; add matching sticky ends to cDNA (or cut with same enzyme); mix so sticky ends pair; DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds; promoter included. (b) The plasmid carries a marker gene such as GFP; colonies that fluoresce under UV light contain the plasmid; (or antibiotic resistance with replica plating).
items.markingKey: (a) same restriction enzyme [1]; complementary sticky ends [1]; ligase [1] [3] (b) marker gene [1]; detection method [1] [2]

items.stem: A company in Dhaka produces human insulin for treating diabetes using genetically modified bacteria. (a) Describe how bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid are identified. (b) Explain the advantages of producing human insulin using genetically modified bacteria.
items.answer: (a) The plasmid carries a marker gene such as GFP; colonies that fluoresce under UV light contain the plasmid; (or antibiotic resistance with replica plating). (b) Identical to human protein so fewer immune reactions; large quantities quickly and cheaply in fermenters; no risk of infection from animal/human sources; no ethical issues of using animals.
items.markingKey: (a) marker gene [1]; detection method [1] [2] (b) any 3 from: Identical to human protein so fewer immune reactions; large quantities quickly and cheaply in fermenters; no risk of infection from animal/human sources; no ethical issues of using animals (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "annealing"?
options: A heat-stable DNA polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, used in PCR because it is not denatured at 95 °C.
A short single-stranded DNA sequence complementary to the end of the target sequence, which allows DNA polymerase to start copying.
The binding of primers to complementary sequences on single-stranded DNA as the mixture cools to about 55–65 °C.
The polymerase chain reaction: a method of making many copies of a specific DNA sequence by cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension.
items.answer: The binding of primers to complementary sequences on single-stranded DNA as the mixture cools to about 55–65 °C.
items.markingKey: Annealing: the binding of primers to complementary sequences on single-stranded DNA as the mixture cools to about 55–65 °C.

items.stem: Describe the three stages of one PCR cycle.
items.answer: Denaturation at 95 °C breaks hydrogen bonds, separating strands; annealing at about 55–65 °C allows primers to bind complementary sequences; extension at 72 °C, Taq polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3′ end of primers to make new strands.
items.markingKey: denaturation [1]; annealing of primers [1]; extension by Taq [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments.
items.answer: DNA is loaded into wells at the cathode end; a current is applied; negatively charged DNA moves towards the anode; agarose gel acts as a sieve, smaller fragments moving faster and further; fragments separate by size; stained or labelled to show bands.
items.markingKey: negative charge to anode [1]; gel as sieve [1]; small move further [1]; visualised [1] [4]

items.stem: Felix amplified a DNA sample from a crime scene in Jakarta. The reaction started with 2 copies of the target sequence and ran for 25 cycles, each lasting 2.5 minutes. Explain why the sample was amplified before DNA profiling.
items.answer: Only a tiny amount of DNA was present; PCR makes enough copies for analysis by electrophoresis.
items.markingKey: Only a tiny amount of DNA was present [1]; PCR makes enough copies for analysis by electrophoresis [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf amplified a DNA sample from a crime scene in Lagos. The reaction started with 5 copies of the target sequence and ran for 30 cycles, each lasting 3 minutes. (a) Calculate the number of copies of the target sequence after all cycles, assuming 100% efficiency. (b) Calculate the total time taken.
items.answer: (a) 5.37 × 10⁹ (b) 90 minutes

items.stem: Leila separated a DNA ladder and an unknown fragment by gel electrophoresis. Ladder fragments (base pairs) and distances moved (cm): 8000 bp 3.7 cm, 5000 bp 4.2 cm, 3000 bp 4.9 cm, 2000 bp 5.4 cm, 1000 bp 6.2 cm. The unknown fragment moved 5.7 cm. (a) Explain why the fragments separate. (b) Describe how the bands are made visible. (c) Explain why the voltage is switched off before the DNA reaches the end of the gel.
items.answer: (a) The gel acts as a mesh; smaller fragments move through it more easily and travel further in the same time. (b) Stain with a DNA dye (e.g. ethidium bromide / SYBR safe) and view under UV, or use radioactive or fluorescent probes. (c) The smallest fragments would run off the gel into the buffer and be lost.
items.markingKey: (a) The gel acts as a mesh [1]; smaller fragments move through it more easily and travel further in the same time [1] [2] (b) Stain with a DNA dye (e.g. ethidium bromide / SYBR safe) and view under UV, or use radioactive or fluorescent probes [1] (c) The smallest fragments would run off the gel into the buffer and be lost [1]

items.stem: A PCR starts with one DNA molecule. How many molecules are present after 5 cycles?
Explain how DNA profiling can show whether a man is the biological father of a child.
items.answer: Each band in the child's profile must come from either the mother or the father; bands in the child not present in the mother must match bands in the father; if they do not, he is not the father.
items.markingKey: half bands from each parent [1]; non-maternal bands compared [1]; conclusion rule [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why primers are needed in PCR.
items.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end; primers provide this and define which section of DNA is copied.
items.markingKey: start point for polymerase [1]; specify target region [1] [2]

items.stem: In a paternity case in Santiago, a single STR locus was analysed by gel electrophoresis. Band sizes (numbers of repeats): mother [7, 19]; child [7, 16]; Man 1 [6, 16]; Man 2 [10, 11]. Determine which man could be the father. Explain your reasoning.
items.answer: Man 1: the child's non-maternal band (16 repeats) matches one of his bands; the other man has neither.
items.markingKey: identifies maternal band [1]; non-maternal band matched to Man 1 [1]; other man excluded [1] [3]

items.stem: In a paternity case in Lima, a single STR locus was analysed by gel electrophoresis. Band sizes (numbers of repeats): mother [5, 16]; child [11, 16]; Man 1 [6, 11]; Man 2 [8, 19]. Determine which man could be the father. Explain your reasoning.
items.answer: Man 1: the child's non-maternal band (11 repeats) matches one of his bands; the other man has neither.
items.markingKey: identifies maternal band [1]; non-maternal band matched to Man 1 [1]; other man excluded [1] [3]

items.stem: Ana separated a DNA ladder and an unknown fragment by gel electrophoresis. Ladder fragments (base pairs) and distances moved (cm): 8000 bp 3.7 cm, 5000 bp 4.2 cm, 3000 bp 4.9 cm, 1000 bp 6.2 cm, 200 bp 8.2 cm. The unknown fragment moved 6.6 cm. (a) Estimate the size of the unknown fragment, explaining your method. (b) Explain why the DNA fragments move through the gel. (c) Describe how the bands are made visible. (d) Explain why the voltage is switched off before the DNA reaches the end of the gel.
items.answer: (a) About 700 bp: plot log(size) against distance for the ladder and read off the size at 6.6 cm. (b) DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups so moves towards the positive electrode (anode) when a voltage is applied. (c) Stain with a DNA dye (e.g. ethidium bromide / SYBR safe) and view under UV, or use radioactive or fluorescent probes. (d) The smallest fragments would run off the gel into the buffer and be lost.
items.markingKey: (a) calibration with ladder [1]; estimate in range 595–804 bp [1] [2] (b) DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups so moves towards the positive electrode (anode) when a voltage is applied [2] [2] (c) Stain with a DNA dye (e.g. ethidium bromide / SYBR safe) and view under UV, or use radioactive or fluorescent probes [1] (d) The smallest fragments would run off the gel into the buffer and be lost [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "somatic gene therapy"?
options: The collection, storage and analysis of biological information, such as DNA and protein sequences, using computers and databases.
Gene therapy in gametes or early embryos, so the change is inherited; not permitted in humans in most countries.
A small glass slide or chip with thousands of different DNA probes fixed in a grid, used to detect which genes are present or expressed in a sample.
Gene therapy in body cells, so the change is not passed to offspring.
items.answer: Gene therapy in body cells, so the change is not passed to offspring.
items.markingKey: Somatic gene therapy: gene therapy in body cells, so the change is not passed to offspring.

items.stem: Describe how a microarray is used to compare gene expression in cancer cells and normal cells.
items.answer: Extract mRNA from both; make cDNA with reverse transcriptase; label with different fluorescent dyes; mix and apply to microarray; cDNA hybridises to complementary probes; scan; colour/intensity of each spot shows relative expression of each gene.
items.markingKey: mRNA → cDNA [1]; different fluorescent labels [1]; hybridisation to probes [1]; scanning / colour interpretation [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why gene therapy for cystic fibrosis has had limited success.
items.answer: Viral vectors/liposomes do not reach enough lung epithelial cells; mucus blocks delivery; immune response to vector; epithelial cells are replaced so treatment must be repeated; inserted gene may be expressed only briefly.
items.markingKey: delivery problems [1]; immune response [1]; cells replaced / repeat treatment [1] [3]

items.stem: Doctors in Manila are considering gene therapy for a patient with cystic fibrosis caused by recessive CFTR alleles. Suggest how gene therapy could be carried out and comment on its likely effectiveness.
items.answer: Deliver functional CFTR alleles to airway epithelial cells using liposomes or a modified virus in an aerosol; cells must be treated repeatedly because epithelial cells are replaced.
items.markingKey: method: vector and target cells [2]; comment on effectiveness [1] [3]

items.stem: cDNA from cancer cells was labelled with a red fluorescent dye and cDNA from normal cells of the same tissue with a green dye. Both were mixed and applied to a microarray. The spots for four genes were: gene P green, gene Q yellow, gene R black, gene S yellow. (a) State what each colour shows about the expression of each gene. (b) State why the two samples were labelled with different dyes.
items.answer: (a) gene P: expressed only (or much more) in the normal cells; gene Q: expressed equally in both; gene R: not expressed in either; gene S: expressed equally in both (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array.
items.markingKey: (a) two correct [1]; all correct [1] [2] (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array [1]

items.stem: A couple in Seoul with a family history of BRCA1 breast cancer risk (dominant allele increasing risk) are offered genetic screening; carriers can choose increased monitoring or preventive surgery. (a) Explain what is meant by pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD). (b) Explain the role of a genetic counsellor.
items.answer: (a) Embryos produced by IVF are tested (one cell removed) for the allele; only unaffected embryos are implanted. (b) Explains the risks and the meaning of test results, options available and supports the couple in making their own informed decision.
items.markingKey: (a) Embryos produced by IVF are tested (one cell removed) for the allele [1]; only unaffected embryos are implanted [1] [2] (b) Explains the risks and the meaning of test results [1]; options available and supports the couple in making their own informed decision [1] [2]

items.stem: What is detected when a spot on a microarray fluoresces brightly after hybridisation with labelled cDNA from a tissue?
options: The tissue has a mutation in that gene
The gene matching that probe is being expressed in the tissue
items.answer: The gene matching that probe is being expressed in the tissue
items.markingKey: cDNA is made from the tissue's mRNA.

items.stem: A microarray spot glows green when cDNA from normal cells is green-labelled and cDNA from tumour cells is red-labelled. What does this show?
options: The gene is absent from the genome
The gene is expressed only in tumour cells
The gene is expressed in normal cells but not (or much less) in tumour cells
The gene is expressed equally in both
items.answer: The gene is expressed in normal cells but not (or much less) in tumour cells
items.markingKey: Green = normal only.

items.stem: Discuss the ethical issues of genetic screening of embryos.
items.answer: Allows parents to avoid serious disease; but may lead to selection of embryos for non-medical traits ("designer babies"); destruction of embryos; discrimination against disabled people; who decides which conditions; cost.
items.markingKey: benefit [1]; two issues [2] [3]

items.stem: Explain how bioinformatics has helped research into malaria.
items.answer: The Plasmodium genome was sequenced and stored in databases; comparing sequences identifies genes for surface antigens and drug resistance; helps design vaccines and drugs.
items.markingKey: genome sequenced / databases [1]; comparisons identify target genes [1]; vaccine / drug design [1] [3]

items.stem: cDNA from cancer cells was labelled with a red fluorescent dye and cDNA from normal cells of the same tissue with a green dye. Both were mixed and applied to a microarray. The spots for four genes were: gene Q black, gene S red, gene U black, gene P yellow. Explain how the cDNA binds to particular spots on the microarray.
items.answer: Each spot contains many copies of a single-stranded probe; cDNA hybridises by complementary base pairing to its matching probe.
items.markingKey: Each spot contains many copies of a single-stranded probe [1]; cDNA hybridises by complementary base pairing to its matching probe [1] [2]

items.stem: Discuss the uses of microarrays, bioinformatics, gene therapy and genetic screening in medicine, and the ethical issues they raise.
items.answer: Microarrays: gene expression profiles, diagnosis, identifying genes; bioinformatics: databases, sequence comparison, drug/vaccine design; gene therapy: viral vectors/liposomes, SCID, CF, somatic vs germ line, limitations; screening: carriers, PGD, prenatal; ethics: consent, discrimination, designer babies, embryo destruction, cost, access.
items.markingKey: microarrays [1]; bioinformatics [1]; gene therapy method [2]; screening [1]; ethics [2] [7]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "rice genetically modified to produce β-carotene (provitamin A) in its endosperm, to reduce vitamin A deficiency"?
items.answer: Golden Rice
items.markingKey: Golden Rice: rice genetically modified to produce β-carotene (provitamin A) in its endosperm, to reduce vitamin A deficiency.

items.stem: Explain how insect pests could become resistant to Bt toxin and how farmers try to prevent this.
items.answer: Random mutations give some insects resistance; Bt crops select for them, so resistance alleles increase; farmers plant refuges of non-Bt crops so susceptible insects survive and mate with resistant ones, diluting resistance alleles.
items.markingKey: mutation and selection [1]; allele frequency increases [1]; refuges [1] [3]

items.stem: In field trials near Mexico City, conventional plants yielded a mean of 7 t ha⁻¹ and needed 3 insecticide sprays per season, while Bt brinjal yielded 9 t ha⁻¹ and needed 0 sprays. Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM crop.

A government agency in Dhaka is deciding whether to allow farmers to grow Golden Rice. (a) Explain why GM crops must be tested before being approved. (b) Suggest one way to reduce the risk of the inserted gene spreading to wild plants.
items.answer: (a) To check that the new protein is not toxic or allergenic to humans or animals and to assess environmental effects such as gene flow. (b) Plant buffer zones; grow where no wild relatives occur; use male-sterile varieties; insert gene into chloroplast DNA (not in pollen).

items.stem: What does the gene inserted into Bt maize code for?
options: A protein that is toxic to some insect larvae
items.answer: A protein that is toxic to some insect larvae

items.stem: In field trials near Kuala Lumpur, conventional plants yielded a mean of 7.5 t ha⁻¹ and needed 3 insecticide sprays per season, while Bt brinjal yielded 8.2 t ha⁻¹ and needed 1 spray. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM crop. (b) Suggest two environmental benefits of using fewer insecticide sprays.
items.answer: (a) 9.3% (b) Less harm to non-target insects (pollinators, predators); less pollution of water; less fuel used; less exposure of farm workers.
items.markingKey: (a) (8.2 − 7.5) ÷ 7.5 × 100 [1] = 9.3% [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Less harm to non-target insects (pollinators, predators); less pollution of water; less fuel used; less exposure of farm workers (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: In field trials near Accra, conventional plants yielded a mean of 5.4 t ha⁻¹ and needed 4 insecticide sprays per season, while Bt brinjal yielded 6.2 t ha⁻¹ and needed 2 sprays. (a) Explain the higher yield and the reduced number of sprays. (b) Suggest why the trial should be repeated over several years and sites.
items.answer: (a) The plants make Bt toxin, killing larvae that eat them, so less damage and more photosynthetic tissue; insecticide is only needed for pests not affected by Bt. (b) Pest numbers and weather vary between years and places; repeats make results more reliable and representative.
items.markingKey: (a) toxin kills feeding larvae [1]; less damage [1]; fewer sprays [1] [3] (b) Pest numbers and weather vary between years and places [1]; repeats make results more reliable and representative [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the genetic code being universal is important for genetic engineering.
items.answer: The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms, so a gene from one organism (e.g. human) is translated into the same protein in another (e.g. bacterium).

items.stem: Doctors in Istanbul are considering gene therapy for a patient with SCID caused by a recessive allele for the enzyme ADA. Suggest how gene therapy could be carried out and comment on its likely effectiveness.
items.answer: Insert a functional ADA allele into the patient's own bone marrow stem cells using a viral vector and return them; stem cells divide to give many T cells with the functional allele; effect can be long-lasting.
items.markingKey: method: vector and target cells [2]; comment on effectiveness [1] [3]

items.stem: A couple in Cairo with a family history of BRCA1 breast cancer risk (dominant allele increasing risk) are offered genetic screening; carriers can choose increased monitoring or preventive surgery. (a) Describe how a person can be screened for a particular allele. (b) Explain the role of a genetic counsellor.
items.answer: (a) Take a sample of cells (blood / cheek swab); extract DNA; amplify the gene by PCR; use a labelled probe, microarray or sequencing to detect the allele. (b) Explains the risks and the meaning of test results, options available and supports the couple in making their own informed decision.

items.stem: Why do farmers growing Bt crops plant refuges of non-Bt crops nearby?
options: To increase the yield of the Bt crop
To slow the evolution of Bt resistance in pests
To provide a source of Bt protein
items.answer: To slow the evolution of Bt resistance in pests
items.markingKey: Susceptible insects mate with resistant ones.

items.stem: Discuss the social and economic issues of growing GM crops in developing countries.
items.answer: Benefits: higher yields, less pesticide cost and exposure, improved nutrition (Golden Rice). Issues: high cost of seed each year; dependence on multinational companies; patents; small farmers may be unable to compete; consumer acceptance and export restrictions.
items.markingKey: benefit [1]; two issues [2] [3]

items.stem: In field trials near Kathmandu, conventional plants yielded a mean of 7.9 t ha⁻¹ and needed 3 insecticide sprays per season, while Bt maize yielded 9 t ha⁻¹ and needed 1 spray. Suggest why the trial should be repeated over several years and sites.
items.answer: Pest numbers and weather vary between years and places; repeats make results more reliable and representative.
items.markingKey: Pest numbers and weather vary between years and places [1]; repeats make results more reliable and representative [1] [2]

items.stem: Why is mRNA often used as a starting point for producing a human gene to put into bacteria?
options: It is more stable than DNA
It has no introns, so bacteria can express the gene
items.answer: It has no introns, so bacteria can express the gene
items.markingKey: Bacteria cannot splice introns; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA.

items.stem: Arjun says: "Human genes can be inserted into bacteria directly from chromosomes and will be expressed." Explain whether Arjun is correct.
items.answer: Human genes contain introns that bacteria cannot remove; cDNA from mRNA is used instead, with a bacterial promoter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Human genes contain introns that bacteria cannot remove; cDNA from mRNA is used instead, with a bacterial promoter. [2]

items.stem: A student in Kuala Lumpur states: "Restriction enzymes join DNA fragments together." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; DNA ligase joins fragments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; DNA ligase joins fragments. [2]

items.stem: A company in Bogotá produces erythropoietin for treating anaemia in kidney disease using genetically modified bacteria. (a) Describe how bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid are identified. (b) Explain the advantages of producing erythropoietin using genetically modified bacteria.
items.answer: (a) The plasmid carries a marker gene such as GFP; colonies that fluoresce under UV light contain the plasmid; (or antibiotic resistance with replica plating). (b) Identical to human protein so fewer immune reactions; large quantities quickly and cheaply in fermenters; no risk of infection from animal/human sources; no ethical issues of using animals.
items.markingKey: (a) marker gene [1]; detection method [1] [2] (b) any 3 from: Identical to human protein so fewer immune reactions; large quantities quickly and cheaply in fermenters; no risk of infection from animal/human sources; no ethical issues of using animals (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: A company in Manila produces erythropoietin for treating anaemia in kidney disease using genetically modified bacteria. (a) Explain why mRNA is extracted from kidney cells rather than using the gene from chromosomal DNA. (b) Explain the advantages of producing erythropoietin using genetically modified bacteria.
items.answer: (a) These cells make the protein so contain many copies of its mRNA; mRNA has no introns, so the cDNA made from it can be expressed by bacteria. (b) Identical to human protein so fewer immune reactions; large quantities quickly and cheaply in fermenters; no risk of infection from animal/human sources; no ethical issues of using animals.

items.stem: Why does DNA move towards the anode in gel electrophoresis?
options: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
items.answer: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
items.markingKey: Phosphates carry negative charge.

items.stem: Sipho says: "In gel electrophoresis, large fragments move faster because they are heavier." Explain whether Sipho is correct.
items.answer: Small fragments move further because they pass through the gel pores more easily.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Small fragments move further because they pass through the gel pores more easily. [2]

items.stem: Tariq amplified a DNA sample from a crime scene in Hanoi. The reaction started with 100 copies of the target sequence and ran for 20 cycles, each lasting 3 minutes. Explain why the sample was amplified before DNA profiling.
items.answer: Only a tiny amount of DNA was present; PCR makes enough copies for analysis by electrophoresis.
items.markingKey: Only a tiny amount of DNA was present [1]; PCR makes enough copies for analysis by electrophoresis [1] [2]

items.stem: In a paternity case in Kathmandu, a single STR locus was analysed by gel electrophoresis. Band sizes (numbers of repeats): mother [16, 19]; child [6, 19]; Man 2 [4, 12]; Man 1 [5, 6]. Determine which man could be the father. Explain your reasoning.
items.answer: Man 1: the child's non-maternal band (6 repeats) matches one of his bands; the other man has neither.
items.markingKey: identifies maternal band [1]; non-maternal band matched to Man 1 [1]; other man excluded [1] [3]

items.stem: Ana separated a DNA ladder and an unknown fragment by gel electrophoresis. Ladder fragments (base pairs) and distances moved (cm): 3000 bp 4.9 cm, 2000 bp 5.4 cm, 1000 bp 6.2 cm, 500 bp 7 cm, 200 bp 8.2 cm. The unknown fragment moved 7.7 cm. (a) Estimate the size of the unknown fragment, explaining your method. (b) Explain why the DNA fragments move through the gel. (c) Explain why the fragments separate. (d) Describe how the bands are made visible.
items.answer: (a) About 300 bp: plot log(size) against distance for the ladder and read off the size at 7.7 cm. (b) DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups so moves towards the positive electrode (anode) when a voltage is applied. (c) The gel acts as a mesh; smaller fragments move through it more easily and travel further in the same time. (d) Stain with a DNA dye (e.g. ethidium bromide / SYBR safe) and view under UV, or use radioactive or fluorescent probes.

items.stem: State two uses of bioinformatics.
items.answer: Comparing DNA/protein sequences between species; identifying genes and predicting protein structure; finding mutations; designing primers; tracking pathogen evolution (e.g. malaria parasite).
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Comparing DNA/protein sequences between species; identifying genes and predicting protein structure; finding mutations; designing primers; tracking pathogen evolution (e.g. malaria parasite) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: cDNA from cancer cells was labelled with a red fluorescent dye and cDNA from normal cells of the same tissue with a green dye. Both were mixed and applied to a microarray. The spots for four genes were: gene P green, gene T yellow, gene U green, gene S red. (a) Explain why cDNA was made from mRNA rather than using genomic DNA. (b) State why the two samples were labelled with different dyes.
items.answer: (a) mRNA is present only for genes being expressed (transcribed); genomic DNA contains all genes whether expressed or not. (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array.
items.markingKey: (a) mRNA shows expression [1]; DNA has all genes [1] [2] (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array [1]

items.stem: cDNA from cancer cells was labelled with a red fluorescent dye and cDNA from normal cells of the same tissue with a green dye. Both were mixed and applied to a microarray. The spots for four genes were: gene S green, gene T yellow, gene R red, gene Q red. (a) State what each colour shows about the expression of each gene. (b) State why the two samples were labelled with different dyes.
items.answer: (a) gene S: expressed only (or much more) in the normal cells; gene T: expressed equally in both; gene R: expressed only (or much more) in the cancer cells; gene Q: expressed only (or much more) in the cancer cells (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array.
items.markingKey: (a) two correct [1]; all correct [1] [2] (b) So that the relative amount of cDNA from each sample binding to each spot can be distinguished on the same array [1]

items.stem: A couple in Dubai with a family history of β-thalassaemia (autosomal recessive) are offered genetic screening; carrier screening is offered before marriage in some countries. (a) Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to the couple of being screened. (b) Explain what is meant by pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD).
items.answer: (a) Advantages: informed decisions about having children (e.g. PGD/IVF), early treatment or monitoring. Disadvantages: anxiety; possible discrimination by insurers/employers; difficult decisions about termination; information about relatives. (b) Embryos produced by IVF are tested (one cell removed) for the allele; only unaffected embryos are implanted.
items.markingKey: (a) advantage [1]; two disadvantages [2] [3] (b) Embryos produced by IVF are tested (one cell removed) for the allele [1]; only unaffected embryos are implanted [1] [2]

items.stem: Glyphosate-resistant soya is sprayed with glyphosate. What happens?
options: Weeds die but the soya survives
Neither weeds nor soya are affected
The soya grows more slowly than the weeds
items.answer: Weeds die but the soya survives
items.markingKey: Resistant EPSPS enzyme.

items.stem: Explain how a crop can be made resistant to the herbicide glyphosate.
items.answer: Glyphosate inhibits an enzyme (EPSPS) needed to make some amino acids; a gene for a bacterial version of the enzyme that is not inhibited is inserted (with a promoter) into the crop, so the crop makes amino acids even when sprayed.
items.markingKey: glyphosate inhibits enzyme [1]; resistant gene from bacterium inserted [1]; plant survives spraying [1] [3]
